Q: Is staging slowly becoming less relevant in modern CI/CD systems? A:

IMO modern CI/CD approaches have become mainstream for quite some time now and while some companies I've worked with have reduced number of environments (I've seen some obscene number of steps/environments set up for testing, like several dev ones for separate teams, then staging than UAT and finally pre-prod) having some kind of staging environment still arguably is a must. It might not be near-perfect (and there are a lot of cases when having it near-perfect is too expensive) but still it's a place where you want to do most of the testing before hitting the production environment, like running automatic (and manual) e2e test suites and so on especially in microservices world, performing some kind of load testing and so on.

Note that still there are quite a lot of systems are shipped as "boxes" where you can't that easily fix something after it was shipped i.e. CD is not that easy.

Another thing to consider is so called "error budgets". Even if we imagine that you have perfect monitoring (which is impossible) and you can do canary or blue/green deployments and have ability to perform blazingly fast rollbacks you still don't want to deploy something which has bugs or something causing noticeable downtime because you still will be performing rollback retrospectively and if you use something like error budget approach (i.e. you have a limit how much customer dissatisfaction your software team is allowed to cause in some timeframe) you can end up blocking your future releases if you have to many faulted ones.

So in a nutshell while an argument can be made that staging slowly becoming less relevant in modern CI/CD systems it still is and will be important/necessary in quite a lot of cases so you don't ship something clearly faulty.
